plans.objective: [DIM: structure] The minimal width $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the constraint matrix formed by the $w$ sample points in a sufficiently rich feature space (e.g., via Fourier or polynomial basis), such that $N_c(w) \ge \text{rank}(\Phi)$, and rigidity is achieved when the feature map is injective on the constraint set.

steps.description: Implement a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that minimal width $N_c(w)$ is determined by the algebraic rank of the constraint matrix $\Phi$ formed by $w$ sample points in a feature space. The workflow will: (1) generate synthetic constraints using a known function $f(x)$; (2) construct the feature matrix $\Phi$ using Fourier/polynomial basis; (3) compute rank($\Phi$); (4) train small feedforward networks of varying widths on $w$ points; (5) evaluate max absolute error on held-out points; (6) identify $N_c(w)$ as the smallest width achieving zero violation (error $\le 10^{-3}$); and (7) compare $N_c(w)$ to rank($\Phi$) to verify if rigidity is achieved when the feature map is injective. All results will be logged with convergence status and error metrics.

steps.description: Design and execute a numerical experiment to probe solution space rigidity using small feedforward networks. Sweep constraint sample count w and hidden width N to find minimal N_c(w) achieving zero-violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3 on held-out constraints). Use a structured grid search over widths [16, 32, 64, 128, 256] and constraint counts w = [10, 20, 50, 100]. Train each configuration with fixed random seeds, measure training and held-out errors, and compute N_c(w) as the smallest width where held-out max error ≤ 1e-3. Test on a synthetic constraint system (e.g., polynomial interpolation or ODE solution points) to ensure ground-truth feasibility. If N_c(w) remains bounded and small as w increases, conclude rigidity; if N_c(w) grows unbounded or stays infinite, conclude fatness.

plans.objective: [DIM: geometry] The function space of solutions to w constraints forms a manifold in the space of continuous functions; N_c(w) corresponds to the minimal width such that the network's feature map can locally embed this manifold without topological obstruction.

steps.description: We will design a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that the solution space to a set of constraints forms a manifold, and that the minimal network width $N_c(w)$ required to achieve zero-violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3 on held-out constraints) scales with the "rigidity" of this space. We will generate a family of constraint sets (e.g., polynomial interpolation, differential equation residuals, or manifold embedding tasks), train small feedforward networks of varying widths, and measure the transition from "fat" (no width achieves zero-violation) to "rigid" (a finite small width suffices). We will sweep $w$ (number of constraints) and $N$ (hidden width), record training/validation errors, and extract $N_c(w)$ as the minimal width satisfying the zero-violation criterion. We will analyze whether $N_c(w)$ saturates or grows with $w$, and compare to the theoretical expectation of a sharp transition.

steps.description: We will conduct a controlled numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that the minimal network width $N_c(w)$ required for zero-violation convergence is dictated by the condition number of the Hessian at the global minimum. (1) Generate constraint functions $f_i(x)$ from a Gaussian process kernel $k(x, x') = \exp(-\|x-x'\|^2 / \gamma^2)$ where the bandwidth $\gamma$ is independently tuned to control the Hessian condition number without altering the number of constraints $w$. (2) Train wide enough networks to ensure convergence to the global minimum (verified by loss landscape flatness checks), then compute the empirical Hessian condition number $\kappa$. (3) Identify $N_c(w)$ via width-sweeping until zero-violation is achieved, and verify scaling laws $N_c \propto \kappa^\alpha$. (4) Compare results against the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) prediction for function-space capacity to distinguish between over-parameterization and conditioning effects.

steps.description: This hypothesis is about neural network capacity and algebraic rank in function space, not a physical/materials problem. Therefore, no DFT/MD/Materials skills apply. Instead, I will design a numerical experiment to test the relationship between constraint count $w$, network width $N$, and zero-violation feasibility. I will use a symbolic regression / sensitivity analysis approach to explore the parameter space and identify the minimal width $N_c(w)$ that satisfies the zero-violation condition (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3 on held-out constraints). The plan involves: (1) generating a set of analytical constraint functions; (2) training small feedforward networks with varying widths; (3) measuring violation on held-out points; (4) determining $N_c(w)$ for each $w$; and (5) assessing whether $N_c$ remains bounded (rigid) or grows unbounded (fat) as $w$ increases. This directly tests the algebraic rank hypothesis in the NTK regime.

steps.description: Design a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that the minimal network width $N_c(w)$ exhibits a phase transition (rigid vs. fat) as a function of constraint count $w$. We will generate synthetic constraint functions (analytic or algebraic) with known solution-space geometry, train small MLPs on $w$ points, and scan hidden widths to find the minimum $N_c(w)$ achieving zero violation (max error $\le 10^{-3}$). The goal is to determine if $N_c(w)$ remains bounded (rigid) or diverges (fat) as $w$ increases, and whether this correlates with manifold dimensionality or NTK complexity. We will use multiple constraint families (low-rank linear, nonlinear manifold, high-curvature) to probe the "if and only if" claim about low-dimensional NTK representation.
